## Why does Morini feel like crying when he goes to see Liz?

Morini wants to cry because the visit to London forces him, in a particularly cruel way, to **recognize his own limitations**.

- **The despair of the body.** Morini has multiple sclerosis and is gradually losing control of his body. In London, with Norton, he feels the pain of **being alive** more intensely than ever. He loves Norton, but knows that his body has already withdrawn from the “competition.” Watching Pelletier and Espinoza, so full of life, able to run and embrace as they please, he experiences a kind of **physical desolation**. He wants to cry because he sees himself as a soul imprisoned in a failing body.

- **The collapse of an ideal.** Of the four, Morini is the most sensitive and the closest to poetry. For him, the London visit carries a kind of end-of-the-world romanticism. But inside Norton's everyday life, abstract literary discussions become concrete moments of awkward care and silence. He realizes that **literature and the life of the mind cannot bridge the body's divide**. His urge to cry comes from discovering that something beautiful, such as his love for Norton, is powerless against reality.

## Why spend hundreds of pages watching professors fall in love?

- **To establish a measure of “civilization” before destroying it.** Bolaño first needs to build an **extremely civilized, refined, even slightly affected** world. The four critics live a typical First World life: they worry about the authenticity of manuscripts, the elegance of rhetoric, clean hotel sheets, and who loves whom more. Only after that world has been given enough substance can their arrival in Santa Teresa, with its **raw, brutal, seemingly senseless violence**, make the collapse of civilization hit so hard. It is like being shown a beautiful piece of porcelain before seeing it thrown into the mud and crushed.

- **To show the intellectual's “spiritual impotence.”** Their love for Archimboldi is a **substitute**. They spend their energy on complicated romances and academic disputes, avoiding reality. Through this long account, Bolaño shows how absorbed these supposedly leading intellectuals are in **games of self-dramatization**, before they encounter real suffering and danger. The length itself reveals the **emptiness** of their lives: having nothing else to do, they circle around the details of their feelings.
